strengths: The paper addresses a problem of clear interest to researchers in program representation learning and reverse engineering: transferring information from source code and descriptions to lower-level code representations.
The combination of a frozen source/comment encoder, a trainable binary encoder, and learned interpolation is a plausible approach. The overview diagram communicates the main training stages clearly.

The evaluation covers four downstream tasks and includes component ablations and a CodeT5 extension. Reported improvements are encouraging: function-name accuracy reaches 33.41 versus 29.41 for RoBERTa, and summarization BLEU-4 reaches 34.36 versus 32.43 for GraphCodeBERT. These results provide a useful starting point, subject to the methodological concerns below.
weaknesses: Necessary—resolve the POJ-104 evaluation protocol. Section 3.2 and Table 2 specify disjoint training/development/test problem labels (64/16/24), while Section 4.2 describes supervised classification into 104 classes. Ordinary closed-set classification cannot learn the held-out labels under this setup. If the experiment is actually retrieval or metric learning, specify its objective, query/candidate construction, ranking cutoff, and metric formulas. This ambiguity affects a main result and most ablations, preventing confident interpretation.

Necessary—align the binary-analysis claims with the evaluated inputs. Sections 3.1–3.2 use compiler-produced LLVM IR, and Figures 7–8 retain informative function names, global symbols, and types. This differs materially from analyzing stripped executables; the footnote describing these representations as trivially interchangeable is inaccurate. Either scope the conclusions to the evaluated LLVM setting and disclose retained information, or supply evidence using representations recovered from stripped executables.

Necessary—make the method reproducible. Equation (4) defines raw averaged similarity matrices as cross-entropy targets, although the surrounding prose says a softmax is applied. Specify the actual target distribution, normalization, gradient flow through targets, and modality-pair sampling. The encoder checkpoints, pooling/projection configuration, interpolation-network implementation, and generation decoders also need concrete specifications. These details determine the implemented algorithm and cannot be recovered reliably from the high-level description.

Necessary—clarify data independence and evaluation targets. Document how the AnghaBench pretraining holdout maps to downstream training, validation, and test sets; Section 3.2 explicitly places generation evaluation on validation data. Describe duplicate and repository-overlap handling across the GitHub-derived corpora. Since comments are generated with CodeT5, identify the provenance of summarization references and distinguish agreement with synthetic descriptions from independently established semantic accuracy. These are unresolved questions, rather than demonstrated leakage.

Necessary—strengthen attribution to interpolation. PCL receives 10 pretraining epochs, whereas the full model receives 30 or 70. The statement that PCL converged does not provide enough evidence to separate the interpolation benefit from additional training. Supply matched-budget or documented convergence comparisons and isolate the linear/nonlinear stages if their individual benefits are claimed. The reported greater-than-97% deterioration under multi-objective training also needs its exact objective and optimization protocol. Limit superiority claims to the tested baselines unless relevant binary-focused comparisons are supplied. Uncertainty estimates are particularly relevant to small differences such as reverse-engineering exact match of 25.16 versus 24.73.

Necessary—correct unsupported semantic and representation-quality conclusions. BLEU, GLEU, and exact match establish textual agreement, but do not establish functional preservation. Figure 8 even presents a positive output containing the syntactically incomplete statement 'do_exit_group(status << );' as printed. Verify the examples and provide compilation/behavioral checks or narrow the claims to textual reconstruction. Likewise, Section 4.1 incorrectly argues that unique programs should not cluster and that t-SNE visualization proves embedding quality; uniqueness does not preclude shared semantics, and separate t-SNE plots cannot establish the claimed geometric improvement.

Optional improvements—streamline the human-learning analogy, describe featurewise interpolation more precisely rather than assuming it remains within the simplex spanned by the original embeddings, and correct inconsistent terminology and references, including GLUE/GLEU, DIRE/DIRT/DIRTY, and the unresolved T5 citation. These editorial improvements would help readability; the recommendation is driven by the substantive evidence and specification concerns above.
